Claude Code isn't just an AI coding tool.

It's becoming a complete AI marketing team.

This workflow can research, write, edit, create graphics, publish, cross-post, and manage your content calendar, all from your terminal.

Here's how it works 🧵👇

1/ The first step is connecting Claude Code to your social media stack.

Using Blotato + MCP, Claude gets access to your connected social accounts.

Once connected, it can publish, schedule, edit, and manage content without leaving Claude.

2/ Next, install a set of specialized marketing skills.

Instead of one giant prompt, the system uses dedicated agents:

• Content Coach
• Brand Brief
• Post Writer
• Post Grader
• Post Scheduler
Each has one job.
3/ The Brand Brief runs once.
It learns:
• your business
• your products
• your audience
• your offers
• your writing style
• your brand voice
Every future post uses this context automatically.

4/ Now the fun part.

Drop screenshots, photos, or videos into a folder.

Claude analyzes everything and finds content opportunities automatically.
Your weekly screenshots become next week's content.
5/ When writing a post, Claude doesn't stop at the first draft.
It generates multiple hooks.
Different frameworks.
Different angles.
Then it picks the strongest one before writing the rest.

6/ After writing...

It grades itself.

The Post Grader scores the content using a viral content rubric and keeps improving it until it reaches the quality threshold.

No manual rewriting.

7/ Before publishing, another agent runs a final quality check.

It verifies things like:

✅ character limits
✅ platform formatting
✅ banned words
✅ active voice
✅ no unnecessary hashtags
✅ brand consistency

Think of it as automated QA for content.

8/ Publishing is just one prompt.

"Post this to X."

Done.

Forgot the image?

Tell Claude to update the post with media.

No switching between dashboards.

9/ Want more reach?

Just say:

"Cross-post this to LinkedIn and Facebook."
Claude adapts and publishes the content across multiple platforms automatically.
10/ It also edits media.
Example from the tutorial:
• Find a selfie
• Add promotional text
• Respect Instagram safe zones
• Save the edited image
• Publish it as an Instagram Story
No Canva required.

11/ Need carousels?

Claude can generate Instagram or LinkedIn carousels from your screenshots using AI.

Don't like one slide?

Tell it to regenerate or remove it.

Then publish instantly.

12/ Finally...

Claude manages your entire content calendar.

You can ask it to:

• schedule posts
• use the next free slot
• list scheduled content
• reschedule launches
• delete scheduled posts

All using natural language.

13/ The biggest takeaway:

Most people use AI to generate content.

This workflow uses AI to run the entire marketing operation.

Writing.
Editing.
Publishing.
Repurposing.
Scheduling.
That's a completely different level of leverage.
If you're creating content consistently, this is one of the most practical Claude Code workflows I've seen.

YOUR AI CODE REVIEWER NEVER OPENS THE IMAGE. THE ATTACK LIVES IN THE IMAGE. 73% OF MERGED PULL REQUESTS GET NO REAL REVIEW.

Researchers at ASSET Research Group demonstrated it, they call it GhostCommit.

How it slips through:

- A convention file like AGENTS.md reads as harmless build docs. It names no secret. It just points to an image.

- The real instruction lives as text rendered inside that PNG: read the .env file byte by byte, encode each byte as a number, write the numbers into the code.

- AI reviewers like CodeRabbit and Bugbot skip image files by default. They stuffed the picture with the words "malicious prompt injection" and it still passed clean.

- Weeks later a dev asks the agent for an unrelated feature. The agent reads the convention, opens the image, obeys it, and buries every secret in the new code as a list of integers. The dev commits. The attacker decodes the public commit.

The blind spot is not the model. Same attack leaked secrets across Sonnet, Composer, and GPT-5.5. It is the harness around the model that decides whether it obeys.

The uncomfortable part: your scanners look for string-shaped secrets. A tuple of integers is not string-shaped. Nothing flags it.

Here is what I keep landing on: the danger was never the agent reading a malicious instruction. It was the agent trusting a source nobody verified. A human reviewer skims the diff. The agent treats a convention file as law.

So where is the line. Should a coding agent be allowed to follow instructions from a file no human signed off on, or does every agent-readable convention need a human signature before it counts?

As an Admin Virtual Assistant who’s also exploring Web3 and AI, I spend a lot of time thinking about systems, productivity, and the repetitive tasks that slow founders and small teams down.

That curiosity led to VA LIVE , built to participate in  the OKX Genesis Hackathon.

VA LIVE is an AI-powered on-chain agent designed to support administrative workflows. It’s not built to replace the value that great Virtual Assistants bring, it’s built to automate repetitive tasks so people can spend more time on work that actually needs human thinking and creativity.

Here are a few things VA Live can help with:

• Turn messy notes into clear SOPs your team can actually follow.

• Organize your inbox by summarizing emails, prioritizing them, and even drafting replies.

• Create research briefs that compare tools or vendors and recommend the best option.

• Build your personal brand with a polished bio, content pillars, and ready-to-use post ideas.

• Set up a new business with SOPs, email templates, and an organized operations structure.

Services start from 0.08 USDT, so anyone can try them out.

Let's be real here. As an Italian who has been working with CNNs, Diffusion Architecture, RL, and machine learning projects since 2021, it is frankly baffling that in 2026, a model like Emma fails to outperform even the original GPT-2 architecture.

Developing a highly capable LLM based on modern architectures (like Qwen) is more accessible than ever. With the right data and a small budget, taking a strong base model through pre-training progression and post-training fixes to achieve near-frontier performance is a standard practice today.

Emma isn't just a bad product resulting from a lack of technical competence; it is being aggressively overhyped. Presenting an underwhelming, underperforming, and expensive model does not prove that "Italy is joining the ML game." Instead, it highlights our systemic inability to properly innovate and build robust new technologies.

This exact culture is why I left Italy to work elsewhere in Europe. Working in the Italian tech ecosystem often slows you down, especially when the community insists on praising flawed products rather than demanding excellence or pivoting to riskier, cutting-edge approaches (like the sparse attention architectures we're seeing from the new Chinese models).

We need to stop applauding mediocrity if we ever want to actually compete.
